topic.title: Variables
topic.description: Declaring and using variables to store data

sections.title: What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Ready to learn **Variables**?

Here's what we'll cover:

• Declaring and using variables to store data
• Why this matters for your coding journey
• Hands-on examples you can try

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
Think of **Variables** like building blocks. 

Every great program starts with small, simple pieces. This is one of those essential pieces!

• Start simple, then build up
• Practice makes it click
• Don't worry if it takes time - totally normal!

sections.title: Code Examples
Key Points
points: A variable must be declared with a type before it can be used
Declaration allocates memory; assignment stores a value in that memory
Variables can be initialized at declaration: int count = 0
Each variable has a type that determines the values it can hold and memory it occupies
A variable must be assigned a value before it is used in an expression

sections.title: Summary
sections.content: Variables - Declaring and using variables to store data. Master basics before advancing. Practice with the examples. Builds foundation for what's next.

questions.question: What happens if you try to use a variable before assigning it a value in Java?
questions.explanation: Java requires local variables to be initialized before use. If you try to use an uninitialized local variable, the compiler will report an error.

questions.question: Which statement correctly declares two integer variables in Java?
options: Both A and B are correct
questions.explanation: Both 'int x, y;' (comma-separated) and separate declarations 'int x; int y;' are valid ways to declare multiple variables of the same type in Java.
